source.text:
Bandit: interleaves explore and exploit, shifting traffic to the better arm in real time (Thompson sampling, UCB). Best when the cost of showing the loser during the test is high and the window is short: headlines, seasonal and holiday promotions, banner creative, product recommendations. Minimises regret rather than delivering a clean estimate; the tradeoff is less certainty about the losing arms and a heavier focus on one KPI.

Ecommerce pattern that has emerged: hybrid. A/B tests for site-wide, high-stakes changes; bandits for high-volume tactical decisions. Bandits need sticky bucketing so returning users stay on one arm. For a $100M/year retailer, most A/B tests reach power within two weeks, so A/B is operationally feasible and bandits are an add-on (leadgen-economy.com). Below a few thousand orders/month, bandits are only justified for short campaigns.

9. prioritisation frameworks

ICE (Sean Ellis / GrowthHackers): Impact, Confidence, Ease, each 1-10, averaged. Fast, subjective. Weakness: whoever pitches the idea also scores it, so everything scores 9/9/9 and nothing gets deprioritised. Best for small teams building the habit.

PIE (Chris Goward / WiderFunnel): Potential, Importance (traffic/value of the page), Ease. 1-10 each. Forces you to look at traffic data. Middle ground.

PXL (Peep Laja / CXL): replaces subjective scores with about 10-14 binary or scaled criteria tied to evidence: is the change above the fold, is it noticeable within 5 seconds, is it on a high-traffic page, is it backed by heatmaps/user testing/surveys/analytics, how hard to build. Weighted, mostly yes/no, which cuts scoring subjectivity. Best for mature programmes. Slowest.

RICE (Intercom): Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort. Adds audience size; good when reach varies.

Prioritise by expected profit, not expected lift. The frameworks above score "impact" loosely. The better objective is expected value = P(win) x expected lift x value per conversion x traffic exposed, minus build cost. A 20% lift on a low-margin, low-traffic page can be worth less than a 5% lift on the checkout of your hero product. For a DTC brand, weight by gross profit per conversion, not revenue, because a conversion lift that shifts mix toward low-margin SKUs can raise revenue and cut profit. Use PXL-style evidence gating (no test enters the backlog without at least 2 points of evidence) plus a profit-weighted ceiling estimate.

10. research process that generates hypotheses

Method only; keep the page-design output in LPG. Each method and what it feeds:

Analytics funnel analysis (GA4, Shopify): find the step with the biggest drop and the most traffic. Feeds where to test.

Session replay: watch real sessions to see rage clicks, dead clicks, loops, form abandonment. Feeds what is confusing.

Heatmaps/scroll maps: see what gets attention and what is missed. Feeds hypotheses about placement and reach. Weight by revenue per click, not raw clicks.

On-site surveys (exit intent, post-purchase): ask why people did not buy or almost did not. Feeds objections.

User testing: watch 5-8 people attempt a task and narrate. Feeds usability problems.

Customer interviews: understand motivation, anxiety, and the words customers use. Feeds messaging hypotheses. The output of research is a prioritised, evidence-backed hypothesis, not a test itself. DRIP reports a 36.3% win rate because it pre-qualifies every hypothesis with analytics, session recordings, and heatmaps before building; teams that test without research see lower win rates.

11. test design

Hypothesis structure: "Because we observed [evidence], we believe [change] will cause [effect] for [segment], measured by [primary metric]. We will know it worked if [metric moves by MDE]." Ties the test to evidence and a decision.

Primary metric choice:

Conversion rate: binary, low variance, fastest to power. Blind spot: ignores order value.

Revenue per visitor (RPV): captures conversion and AOV together. But revenue is highly skewed: in a typical ecommerce case 97% of visitors spend $0, a few spend a lot, so the coefficient of variation can be around 750% (sd $18 on a mean of $2.40). This needs roughly 6x the traffic of a conversion-rate test for the same relative MDE (about 175,000 vs 28,000 per variant at a 3% baseline).

Gross profit per visitor: the honest objective for a DTC brand, because it prices in margin and discounting. Same variance problem as RPV, plus margin data.

Why revenue metrics need more sample: variance of order value adds to the binary conversion variance. Mitigate by winsorizing outlier orders or using a threshold proportion metric (share of visitors who spend more than $X) so no single large order dominates.

Guardrail metrics: metrics that must not get worse even if the primary improves: AOV, return rate, refund rate, page load, add-to-cart, margin. A conversion win that tanks AOV or margin is not a win.

Test duration: at least one full week, in practice two, plus enough to hit the pre-computed sample size. Do not stop just because you hit significance early.

Device and traffic-source splits: mobile and desktop convert differently and can move in opposite directions; a blended win can hide a mobile loss. Pre-register these as segments rather than fishing. Same for paid vs organic, new vs returning.

12. ecommerce and Shopify-specific constraints (2025-2026)

Checkout. Since Shopify rolled out checkout extensibility to all merchants (checkout.liquid deprecated; general rollout August 2024), direct JavaScript injection into checkout is gone. Third-party client-side tools can no longer A/B test the checkout UI by injecting JS, and Shopify's own developer forum confirms there is no built-in way to show a customisation to one group and hide it from another via extensibility rules. So classic client-side checkout A/B testing is not possible on standard Shopify. What you can still test:

Non-Plus plans (Basic, Shopify, Advanced): everything before checkout: product pages, collection pages, cart, homepage, add-to-cart, trust badges, pricing display. Varify and similar run via a head snippet on all plans.

Shopify Plus: checkout extensibility (Checkout Blocks, UI extensions, Shopify Functions, Branding API) plus native theme A/B testing. Some apps (Personizely, Checkout Boost) run limited checkout-element tests via Checkout Blocks on Plus. About 80% of high-impact ecommerce tests happen before checkout anyway. Theme testing. Shopify's native "Rollouts" does server-side theme A/B testing: the split happens on Shopify's servers before the page ships, so there is no flicker and no speed penalty. It reports numbers but gives no significance verdict, so the statistical judgment is yours (usestorepilot.com; requires a paid plan tier). Price testing. Legal in the US and EU provided the price difference is not based on protected characteristics (nationality, gender, race), which is negative price discrimination and illegal. Showing two different prices for the identical product to different users at the same time is legal in most places but is an ethics and brand landmine. Amazon's September 2000 DVD price test is the cautionary case: per Amazon's own statement it tested discount levels of 20% to 40% on 68 DVD titles over five days; after customers compared notes and backlash followed, Amazon refunded 6,896 customers an average of $3.10 each (about $21,377 total, ABC News, September 29 2000), and Bezos said "we've never tested and we never will test prices based on customer demographics... even that was a mistake because it created uncertainty for customers." Amazon still refuses personalised pricing. The EU requires disclosure when a price is personalised. Safer practice: test price presentation, framing, tiers, and bundles rather than the raw number for the same SKU; or test different offerings (add/remove a feature) at different prices. Dedicated Shopify price-test apps exist (TestSignal). Tooling landscape after Google Optimize (sunset September 30 2023). No native Google replacement; Google now points to partners AB Tasty, Optimizely, VWO. Current landscape:

Client-side visual editors: VWO (free up to 50,000 tested users/mo), AB Tasty, Convert.com, Kameleoon, Optimizely Web.

Engineering-led / server-side / feature-flag: GrowthBook (open source, self-host free), Statsig (free up to 1M events/mo; powers OpenAI, Notion, Atlassian), Eppo (warehouse-native), Split, LaunchDarkly.

Shopify-native: Shopify Rollouts (theme), plus app-store tools. How they handle stats: Optimizely mSPRT always-valid + FDR; VWO/AB Tasty Bayesian; Statsig sequential; Eppo Bayesian + GAVI; GrowthBook both + sequential + CUPED. Server-side vs client-side tradeoffs:

Client-side: runs in the browser via JS/DOM manipulation. Pros: marketers own it, visual editor, fast to ship. Cons: flicker risk, adds JS payload and slows the page, easier to break, logic is public. AB Tasty: flicker "is caused by the basic client-side operation of A/B testing solutions that apply a JavaScript overlayer during page loading" and there is "no miracle fix."

Server-side: the server or edge decides the variant before render. Pros: no flicker, faster, robust across devices, can test backend logic (pricing, search, recommendations, checkout), works with feature flags. Cons: needs engineers and a deploy cycle, higher cost, slower to ship. GrowthBook: server-side "avoids any issues with flickering that can happen with client side testing." Rule for DTC: use client-side for front-end visual tests on product/cart/home pages; use server-side (or Shopify Rollouts) for anything touching checkout, pricing logic, or performance-sensitive paths.

13. reading results

Confidence intervals over p-values. A CI shows the plausible range of the effect and its magnitude; a bare p-value collapses that to a yes/no at an arbitrary cliff. Report the interval.
